pos: n. (a hiding of what one is; feigning; hypocrisy in the affections — rendering Greek hupokrisis)
etymology: Latin dissimulatio, from dissimulare, to make unlike, to disguise. It is the twin of simulation: simulation pretends what is not, dissimulation conceals what is.
biblical_def: Dissimulation is love wearing a face it does not own. Paul commands its opposite in the plainest terms: “Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good” (Rom 12:9). The Greek is anupokritos — unhypocritical, unmasked — and the two clauses that follow show what unfeigned love does: it hates what is evil and holds fast what is good. Love that cannot abhor is dissimulation already, since it is pretending to approve what it does not. The word's other appearance names the most famous case in the New Testament. At Antioch Peter ate freely with the Gentiles until certain came from James, “he withdrew and separated himself, fearing them which were of the circumcision” (Gal 2:12), “insomuch that Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation” (Gal 2:13). Peter's doctrine was sound; his table was a lie. And Paul's answer defines the sin exactly: he saw “that they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel” (Gal 2:14) and rebuked Peter publicly. Dissimulation is therefore not a private inconsistency but a gospel matter, because what a man does at the table preaches, and Peter's withdrawal preached that Gentiles were second-class in the church of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dissimulation as the act of dissembling; a hiding under a false appearance; a feigning; false pretension; hypocrisy.
webster_full: DISSIMULA'TION, n. The act of dissembling; a hiding under a false appearance; a feigning; false pretension; hypocrisy.
2. Dissimulation may be simply concealment of the opinions, sentiments or purpose; but it includes also the assuming of a false or counterfeit appearance which conceals the real.
DISSEM'BLE, v.t. To hide under a false appearance; to conceal; to disguise; to pretend that not to be which really is.
DISSEM'BLER, n. One who dissembles; a hypocrite; one who conceals his opinions or dispositions under a false appearance.
scriptures: Romans 12:9
Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good.
Galatians 2:12
For before that certain came from James, he did eat with the Gentiles: but when they were come, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing them which were of the circumcision.
Galatians 2:13
And the other Jews dissembled likewise with him; insomuch that Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation.
Galatians 2:14

But when I saw that they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel, I said unto Peter before them all, If thou, being a Jew, livest after the manner of Gentiles, and not as do the Jews, why compellest thou the Gentiles to live as do the Jews?
corruption_summary: Feigned agreement is renamed as kindness or peacekeeping, and the plain rebuke that Scripture requires is treated as the greater sin.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 2 is the standing refutation of the idea that concealing one's real conviction to avoid friction is a form of love. Peter did exactly that — he withdrew, fearing them of the circumcision — and Paul calls it walking not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel, and rebukes an apostle before them all. Note what Peter did not do: he did not teach error. He simply moved his seat. The lesson is that conduct is doctrine in public form, and a man may deny with his table what he affirms in his creed.

Romans 12:9 forbids the other common shape of the sin. Where love is defined as unbroken affirmation, abhorring evil becomes unloving by definition, and Christians learn to smile at what God hates. Paul writes the two commands as one sentence because they are one thing: love without dissimulation abhors evil and cleaves to good. A love that cannot recoil has already begun to pretend, and pretence is what the word means.

The third corruption is the loss of the public rebuke. Paul withstood Peter to the face, before them all, because the offence was public and the injured party was the whole Gentile church. Where every correction must be private and gentle regardless of the injury, dissimulation is protected by procedure, and the strong are shielded from the only remedy Scripture gives. Barnabas — a good man, full of the Holy Ghost — was carried away, which shows how fast the contagion moves when no one speaks.
roots_summary: Greek hupokrisis (G5272), the acting of a part on the stage, hence dissimulation; anupokritos (G505), unfeigned, without dissimulation — the standard for love in Romans 12:9.
roots_lines: Greek hupokrisis (G5272) — the playing of a part; Galatians 2:13, Matthew 23:28, 1 Timothy 4:2.
Greek anupokritos (G505) — unhypocritical, unfeigned; Romans 12:9, 2 Corinthians 6:6, 1 Peter 1:22 of love, and James 3:17 of wisdom.
Greek sunupokrinomai (G4942) — to join in playing a part; Galatians 2:13 of the other Jews dissembling with Peter.
Latin dissimulare, to make unlike — the concealing of what is, as distinct from simulation, the feigning of what is not.
Romans 12:9 gives the two marks of unfeigned love: it abhors evil and cleaves to good.
usage: “Let love be without dissimulation” — and then, abhor evil, cleave to good.
“He withdrew and separated himself, fearing them” — sound doctrine, lying table.
“Barnabas also was carried away” — the contagion takes good men first.

pos: n. (service performed only while watched — rendering Greek ophthalmodouleia)
etymology: A compound coined to render the Greek ophthalmodouleia, literally eye-slavery: work that needs an eye upon it to happen at all.
biblical_def: Eyeservice is work done because someone is looking. Paul uses the word twice, both times to servants, and both times he answers it with the same doctrine. “Not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but as the servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart” (Eph 6:6). “Servants, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh; not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but in singleness of heart, fearing God” (Col 3:22). The cure is not better supervision but a different Master: “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23), and “with good will doing service, as to the Lord, and not to men” (Eph 6:7). Notice how thoroughly this transforms ordinary labour. A bondservant in a heathen household, with no rights, no wages, and no prospect of advancement, is told that his work is rendered to Christ and will be rewarded by Christ. That is not a sedative; it is a promotion. It also removes every excuse. If the labour is offered to the Lord, then the quality of the master, the fairness of the terms, and the presence or absence of an overseer have nothing to do with the standard. The eye that matters never leaves the room.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines eye-service as service performed only under inspection, or the eye of an employer; work done to please by appearance rather than by fidelity.
webster_full: EYE-SERVICE, n. Service performed only under the eye of an employer, or when he is present; work done for appearance rather than from fidelity.
MEN-PLEA'SER, n. One who is solicitous to please men, rather than to please God.
SERV'ICE, n. The act of serving; labor performed for the benefit of another.
SIN'GLENESS, n. Simplicity; sincerity; purity of mind or purpose; freedom from duplicity.
scriptures: Ephesians 6:6
Not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but as the servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart;
Colossians 3:22
Servants, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh; not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but in singleness of heart, fearing God:
Colossians 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
Ephesians 6:7
With good will doing service, as to the Lord, and not to men:
corruption_summary: Work is treated as a transaction with an employer alone, so that fidelity is owed only in proportion to pay, fairness, or observation.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern account of work is contractual: a man owes his employer exactly what was bargained for, and where the bargain is unjust he owes proportionally less. Paul writes to men whose bargain was slavery — the most unjust arrangement possible — and tells them to serve heartily as to the Lord. He does not thereby bless the arrangement; in the same breath he warns masters that they too have a Master in heaven, and elsewhere he tells a bondman to use freedom if he can get it. But he refuses to let the injustice of the terms become the standard of the work, because the work is now rendered to Christ, and Christ is not underpaying anyone.

The second corruption is the reduction of Christian ethics to what can be observed. Where accountability is external only — audits, cameras, reviews — the effect is the very thing Paul names: eyeservice, done well while watched. Singleness of heart, fearing God, is a different mechanism entirely. It produces the same quality of work in an empty room as in a full one, and it is the only mechanism that does. This is not merely a workplace matter; it is the difference between a religion of appearance and a religion of the heart, and Paul locates it in the daily labour of the lowest man in the household.
roots_summary: Greek ophthalmodouleia (G3787), eye-service, work that requires watching — Ephesians 6:6 and Colossians 3:22 only; anthropareskos (G441), men-pleaser.
roots_lines: Greek ophthalmodouleia (G3787) — literally eye-slavery; Ephesians 6:6 and Colossians 3:22, its only occurrences.
Greek anthropareskos (G441) — man-pleaser; the companion word in both verses.
Greek haplotes (G572) — singleness, simplicity of heart; Colossians 3:22, 2 Corinthians 11:3.
The compound is apparently Paul's own coinage; no earlier Greek use is known, and the church has needed it ever since.
The remedy in both passages is a change of Master, not a change of supervision.
usage: “Not with eyeservice, as menpleasers” — the work that stops when the door closes.
“Do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” — the whole cure in one clause.
“In singleness of heart, fearing God” — the eye that never leaves the room.

pos: n. pl. (those who live to please men — rendering Greek anthropareskoi)
etymology: A compound rendering Greek anthropareskos, from anthropos (man) and aresko (to please). The Authorized Version keeps the compound rather than diluting it.
biblical_def: Menpleasers names a whole way of living, and Scripture sets it directly against the service of Christ. Servants are told to work “not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but as the servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart” (Eph 6:6), and “in singleness of heart, fearing God” (Col 3:22). Paul applies the same test to his own ministry, and states the alternatives without a middle term: “For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ” (Gal 1:10). That sentence admits no compromise; the man-pleaser and the servant of Christ are two different men. He says it again of the preaching itself: “as we were allowed of God to be put in trust with the gospel, even so we speak; not as pleasing men, but God, which trieth our hearts” (1Th 2:4). Scripture does not forbid pleasing men in every sense — Paul elsewhere says he pleased all men in all things for their profit, that they might be saved. The sin is in the direction of accountability. The man-pleaser takes his verdict from the room; the servant of Christ takes it from God, who trieth the hearts, and therefore may sometimes displease the room in order to profit it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a men-pleaser as one who is solicitous to please men, rather than to please God; one who seeks the favor of men at the expense of duty.
webster_full: MEN-PLEA'SER, n. One who is solicitous to please men, rather than to please God.
PLEASE, v.t. To excite agreeable sensations or emotions in; to gratify.
2. To satisfy; to content; as, we cannot please all men.
PLEA'SING, ppr. Gratifying; giving satisfaction; and hence, in a moral sense, seeking the favor of another as the rule of conduct.
scriptures: Ephesians 6:6
Not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but as the servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart;
Colossians 3:22
Servants, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh; not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but in singleness of heart, fearing God:
Galatians 1:10
For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.
1 Thessalonians 2:4
But as we were allowed of God to be put in trust with the gospel, even so we speak; not as pleasing men, but God, which trieth our hearts.
corruption_summary: The approval of the audience is made the measure of faithfulness, and a ministry is judged by whether it is received rather than by whether it is true.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 1:10 is the verse every pulpit needs nailed to it. Paul puts the two services side by side and says they cannot be held together: if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ. That is not a caution against being agreeable; it is a statement that the two accountabilities exclude one another at the point where they conflict. A preacher who has never said anything his hearers did not want to hear has no evidence that he is preaching to them at all, and 1 Thessalonians 2:4 supplies the reason: the gospel was put in trust with him, and trustees answer to the owner, not to the crowd.

The corruption spreads well past the pulpit. A church that measures its faithfulness by attendance, reputation, and the absence of offence has taken its verdict from men; a Christian who edits his convictions by the room he is in has done the same on a smaller scale. Ephesians and Colossians show that the disease begins at the level of daily work and ordinary obedience — the servant who performs while watched is a man-pleaser in miniature, and the preacher who trims a doctrine to keep a hearer is the same man grown large. The cure in every case is the same: fear God, who trieth the hearts.
roots_summary: Greek anthropareskos (G441), man-pleaser — Ephesians 6:6, Colossians 3:22; aresko (G700), to please; peitho (G3982), to persuade, in Galatians 1:10.
roots_lines: Greek anthropareskos (G441) — a pleaser of men; Ephesians 6:6 and Colossians 3:22 only.
Greek aresko (G700) — to please; Galatians 1:10, Romans 15:1-3 where Christ pleased not Himself.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test and approve; 1 Thessalonians 2:4, where God is the one who trieth the hearts.
Scripture forbids man-pleasing as a rule of life, not every act of pleasing men; 1 Corinthians 10:33 pleases all men for their profit, that they may be saved.
The dividing question is always whose verdict is final.
usage: “If I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ” — no middle term is offered.
“Not as pleasing men, but God, which trieth our hearts” — trustees answer to the owner.
The man-pleaser takes his verdict from the room.

pos: n. pl. (grudging ill-will at another's good — rendering Greek phthonoi and zeloi)
etymology: Latin invidia, from invidere, to look against, to look upon with ill-will. The Greek phthonos is ill-will at another's advantage; it wants the other man to have less.
biblical_def: Envyings in the plural is one of the works of the flesh, and Paul twice lists it among the sins that wreck churches. Writing to Corinth he fears to find “debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults” (2Co 12:20) — eight words, every one of them a sin of the assembly rather than of the street. In Galatians the verdict is heavier: “Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like: of the which I tell you before, as I have also told you in time past, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God” (Gal 5:21). Envy sits in that list beside murder, and Scripture puts them together elsewhere too, because envy is the seed of which murder is the fruit: Cain, Joseph's brethren, and the chief priests who delivered Christ for envy. James names its effect on a congregation: “where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work” (Jas 3:16). And Paul traces it to its root: “Let us not be desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another” (Gal 5:26). Envy grows in the soil of vainglory. A man who must be reckoned first will resent every brother God blesses, and the resentment is not toward the gift but toward the Giver's distribution.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines envy as pain, uneasiness, mortification or discontent excited by the sight of another's superiority or success, accompanied with some degree of hatred and a desire to depress him.
webster_full: EN'VY, n. Pain, uneasiness, mortification or discontent excited by the sight of another's superiority or success, accompanied with some degree of hatred or malignity, and often with a desire or an effort to depress him.
2. Rivalry; competition.
EN'VY, v.t. To feel uneasiness, mortification or discontent, at the sight of another's superiority or success; to repine at another's prosperity.
EN'VYINGS, n. plural. In the Scriptures, the repeated actings of envy, reckoned among the works of the flesh.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 12:20

For I fear, lest, when I come, I shall not find you such as I would, and that I shall be found unto you such as ye would not: lest there be debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults:
Galatians 5:21
Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like: of the which I tell you before, as I have also told you in time past, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God.
Galatians 5:26
Let us not be desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another.
James 3:16
For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work.
corruption_summary: Envy is renamed as a concern for fairness, so that the desire to see another brought down passes for a demand that things be made right.
corruption_paragraphs: Envy has learned to speak the language of justice, and the disguise is nearly perfect because both are exercised about inequality. The difference is in what would satisfy. Justice is content when the wrong is righted and the poor man is fed; envy is not content until the other man has less. Scripture keeps the categories apart: it commands care for the widow, the fatherless and the stranger, and it forbids envy in the same law. Where a movement's demands would not be satisfied by the raising of the low but only by the pulling down of the high, the name for it is the one in Galatians 5:21.

The churchly form is quieter and just as deadly. Paul's Corinthian list — debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults — is a portrait of an assembly, not a marketplace, and James says the result is confusion and every evil work. Galatians 5:26 gives the root: vainglory. Where men measure themselves against one another rather than against Christ, every brother's gift becomes a rebuke, and the flesh answers a rebuke with resentment. The remedy is not to pretend the gifts are equal but to remember who distributed them, dividing to every man severally as He will.
roots_summary: Greek phthonos (G5355), ill-will at another's good; zelos (G2205), zeal or jealousy according to context; eritheia (G2052), factious intrigue.
roots_lines: Greek phthonos (G5355) — envy, ill-will; Galatians 5:21, Mark 15:10 where the chief priests delivered Christ for envy.
Greek zelos (G2205) — zeal, and in a bad sense jealousy; 2 Corinthians 12:20, James 3:16.
Greek eritheia (G2052) — self-seeking faction; the companion sin in the same lists.
Latin invidere, to look against — envy is a way of looking at a brother.
Envy and murder stand side by side in Galatians 5:21 because the one is the seed of the other.
usage: “Debates, envyings, wraths, strifes” — every item a sin of the assembly.
“Where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work”.
“Let us not be desirous of vain glory” — the root beneath the envy.

pos: n. pl. (quarrels, conflicts — rendering Greek machai)
etymology: From Old English feohtan, to fight. The Greek mache is a battle, and in the epistles it is used of controversies and quarrels among men, not of armies.
biblical_def: Fightings is the Authorized Version's word for quarrels, and James traces them to their source with a surgeon's directness: “From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?” (Jas 4:1). The answer is given as a question because it is obvious once asked. The war outside is the overflow of a war inside; men quarrel because their desires are at war within them and cannot be satisfied. He presses further: “Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have, and cannot obtain: ye fight and war, yet ye have not, because ye ask not” (Jas 4:2). The diagnosis ends in an astonishing place — the quarrelling is finally a failure of prayer, a determination to seize by force what God gives to asking. Paul uses the word of external opposition: “without were fightings, within were fears” (2Co 7:5), the whole condition of a servant of God in a hostile city, harassed outwardly and afraid inwardly. James sets the alternative: “the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace of them that make peace” (Jas 3:18). Fightings produce nothing; peace is the soil in which righteousness is sown, and it must be made by someone.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fighting as contending in battle or in single combat; and, in the plural, contests, quarrels or contentions between persons.
webster_full: FIGHT'ING, ppr. Contending in battle; contending in single combat; striving.
FIGHT'INGS, n. plural. Contentions; quarrels; contests between persons; in the Scriptures, the strifes that arise among brethren from their own lusts.
FIGHT, n. A battle; an engagement; a contest in arms.
2. A struggle or contention of any kind.
scriptures: James 4:1
From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?
James 4:2
Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have, and cannot obtain: ye fight and war, yet ye have not, because ye ask not.
2 Corinthians 7:5
For, when we were come into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest, but we were troubled on every side; without were fightings, within were fears.
James 3:18
And the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace of them that make peace.
corruption_summary: Quarrels are blamed on circumstances, personalities, or the other party, and the internal war James names as the cause is never examined.
corruption_paragraphs: James asks where fightings come from and refuses every external answer. Not from the difficulty of the situation, not from the other man's temperament, not from a failure of communication, but from your lusts that war in your members. This locates the fault where the offender can actually reach it. A church that treats every conflict as a management problem, to be resolved by process, will produce a peace that lasts until the next unmet desire. The apostolic remedy is mortification and prayer, and it begins with a man admitting that he wanted something and did not get it.

The second corruption is the reverse: a false peace that suppresses conflict without dealing with the lust. James 3:18 does not say the fruit of righteousness is sown by avoiding fights; it says it is sown in peace, by those who make peace — an active labour, undertaken by someone who is willing to be the one who moves. Paul's without were fightings, within were fears shows the third thing worth naming: not every conflict is the church's own fault. There is opposition from outside that no amount of self-examination will dissolve, and the apostle's comfort in that case came by God, who comforteth those that are cast down.
roots_summary: Greek mache (G3163), a battle, and by figure a quarrel or controversy — James 4:1, 2 Corinthians 7:5, 2 Timothy 2:23, Titus 3:9.
roots_lines: Greek mache (G3163) — fighting, controversy; James 4:1, 2 Corinthians 7:5, 2 Timothy 2:23, Titus 3:9.
Greek machomai (G3164) — to quarrel, dispute; James 4:2, Acts 7:26, John 6:52.
Greek polemos (G4171) — war; the companion word in James 4:1, the larger conflict beside the smaller.
Greek strateuomai (G4754) — to war as a soldier; James 4:1 of the lusts that war in the members.
James makes prayerlessness the last cause of quarrelling: ye have not, because ye ask not.
usage: “From whence come wars and fightings among you?” — and the answer is inside.
“Ye have not, because ye ask not” — the quarrel is a failure of prayer.
“Without were fightings, within were fears” — not every conflict is self-inflicted.

pos: adj. (out of order; excessive; passion loosed from its rule — rendering Greek pathos)
etymology: Latin inordinatus, not ordered, from in- (not) and ordinare (to set in order). The word does not mean strong; it means unruled.
biblical_def: Inordinate means out of its appointed order, and the word is exact. Paul commands, “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry” (Col 3:5), and adds the reason: “For which things' sake the wrath of God cometh on the children of disobedience” (Col 3:6). The Greek pathos is passion that has slipped its bounds — an affection is not condemned for existing but for ruling where it should serve. Ezekiel uses the word of a nation's spiritual adultery: Aholibah “was more corrupt in her inordinate love than she, and in her whoredoms more than her sister in her whoredoms” (Eze 23:11). John describes the same disorder as the shape of the world itself: “all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world” (1Jn 2:16). This is why Paul ends his list with covetousness, which is idolatry. Inordinate affection is a worship disorder before it is a moral one. Every desire God made has a place and a proportion; when a good thing is loved above its station it becomes a god, and it will exact worship.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines inordinate as irregular; disorderly; excessive; immoderate; not limited to rules prescribed, or to usual bounds.
webster_full: INOR'DINATE, a. Irregular; disorderly; excessive; immoderate; not limited to rules prescribed, or to usual bounds; as inordinate desires.
2. Not according to order or rule; as an inordinate affection.
INOR'DINATELY, adv. Irregularly; excessively; immoderately.
AFFEC'TION, n. The state of being affected; a bent of mind toward a particular object; passion; love.
scriptures: Colossians 3:5
Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry:
Ezekiel 23:11
And when her sister Aholibah saw this, she was more corrupt in her inordinate love than she, and in her whoredoms more than her sister in her whoredoms.
Colossians 3:6
For which things' sake the wrath of God cometh on the children of disobedience:
1 John 2:16
For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.
corruption_summary: Intensity of desire is treated as its own justification, so that a passion strong enough to be called authentic is thereby held to be permitted.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning moral rule of the age is that a desire deeply felt is a desire that must be honoured, and to deny it is to deny the self. Colossians 3:5 answers with a verb: mortify. Paul does not ask whether the affection is sincerely held; he classes inordinate affection with fornication and covetousness and orders it put to death. The word inordinate is precise about the fault. It is not that the desire is intense but that it has left its order — it has taken a place above the God who gave it, and Paul names that place correctly when he calls covetousness idolatry.

The opposite error is the ancient one of treating the affections themselves as the problem, as though the cure for disordered love were less love. Scripture never says so. The remedy for inordinate affection is ordered affection: love God with all the heart, then love the neighbour, then love the wife as Christ loved the church — a hierarchy in which each love is given its proper measure and none is starved. A man is not saved by feeling less; he is saved by loving rightly, and that reordering is the work of the Spirit in sanctification, which is why the command to mortify is addressed to men who are already risen with Christ.
roots_summary: Greek pathos (G3806), passion, inordinate affection — Colossians 3:5, Romans 1:26, 1 Thessalonians 4:5; epithumia (G1939), strong desire, concupiscence.
roots_lines: Greek pathos (G3806) — passion, inordinate affection; Colossians 3:5, Romans 1:26, 1 Thessalonians 4:5.
Greek epithumia (G1939) — desire, longing, in a bad sense lust; the companion word rendered evil concupiscence.
Greek pleonexia (G4124) — covetousness, the desire for more; Colossians 3:5, identified there with idolatry.
Latin inordinatus — not that the affection is too strong, but that it is out of its order.
Ezekiel 23:11 applies the word to a nation's religion; disordered love is idolatry before it is immorality.
usage: “Mortify therefore… inordinate affection” — the command is a verb, not a caution.
“Covetousness, which is idolatry” — the disorder is a worship disorder.
The fault is not intensity but station: a good thing loved above its place.

pos: n. (settled ill-will; badness of disposition — rendering Greek kakia)
etymology: Latin malitia, badness, from malus, evil. The Greek kakia is depravity considered as a disposition — not a deed done but a bent to do harm.
biblical_def: Maliciousness is the settled disposition to do harm, and Paul lists it in the indictment of fallen man: “Being filled with all unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, covetousness, maliciousness; full of envy, murder, debate, deceit, malignity; whisperers” (Rom 1:29). The Greek word describes a bent rather than an act — what a man is disposed to do when he can. Peter uses it with a warning that reaches into the church: “As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, but as the servants of God” (1Pe 2:16). Christian liberty is real, and Peter grants it in the same sentence in which he forbids its abuse; the danger is that freedom becomes a covering under which old dispositions operate unchallenged. He therefore commands its removal at the head of a list: “laying aside all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all evil speakings” (1Pe 2:1). And Paul reminds Titus that this was once the believer's own condition: “we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another” (Tit 3:3). That memory is the great preservative against malice toward others; a man who knows what he was cannot despise what another still is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines maliciousness as the quality of being malicious; extreme enmity or disposition to injure; malignity; and malice as enmity of heart, deliberate and settled.
webster_full: MALI'CIOUSNESS, n. The quality of being malicious; extreme enmity or disposition to injure; malignity.
MAL'ICE, n. Extreme enmity of heart, or malevolence; a disposition to injure others without cause, from mere personal gratification or from a spirit of revenge.
MALI'CIOUS, a. Harboring ill will or enmity without provocation; malevolent in the extreme.
CLOKE, n. A cover; that which conceals; a pretext; an excuse.
scriptures: Romans 1:29
Being filled with all unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, covetousness, maliciousness; full of envy, murder, debate, deceit, malignity; whisperers,
1 Peter 2:16
As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, but as the servants of God.
1 Peter 2:1
Wherefore laying aside all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all evil speakings,
Titus 3:3
For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another.
corruption_summary: Liberty is made a cover for old dispositions, so that unkindness practised in the name of freedom or of truth is never called what Scripture calls it.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter's phrase — a cloke of maliciousness — describes a permanent temptation of free men. Christian liberty is genuine; Peter says as free without qualification before he restricts anything. But liberty makes an excellent covering, because a man doing harm under a banner of principle need never examine his heart. The modern forms are easy to name: contempt expressed as candour, cruelty defended as truth-telling, faction dressed as conviction. Peter's test is whether the freedom is being exercised as the servants of God, and a servant does not get to choose his own object.

Titus 3:3 supplies the antidote and it is memory. Paul does not tell believers to think well of the malicious; he tells them to remember that this is what they themselves were — foolish, disobedient, deceived, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another — and that what changed it was not their own improvement but the kindness and love of God our Saviour appearing. A church that forgets its own former state will grow hard toward the world, and hardness toward the world is maliciousness wearing a doctrinal coat.
roots_summary: Greek kakia (G2549), badness of disposition, malice — Romans 1:29, 1 Peter 2:1, 2:16, Ephesians 4:31; kakoetheia (G2550), malignity, the ill-natured reading of others.
roots_lines: Greek kakia (G2549) — depravity, malice, ill-will; Romans 1:29, 1 Peter 2:1 and 2:16, Colossians 3:8.
Greek kakoetheia (G2550) — malignity, bad character that construes everything to the worst; Romans 1:29.
Greek epikalumma (G1942) — a covering, cloke; 1 Peter 2:16, its only occurrence.
Latin malitia — badness; the word describes a disposition rather than a single deed.
Titus 3:3 uses the cognate kakia of the believer's own former life, which is why malice toward others is inexcusable in him.
usage: “Not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness” — free, and still a servant.
“Laying aside all malice, and all guile” — the first item on Peter's list.
“We ourselves also were sometimes… hateful, and hating one another” — memory is the antidote.

pos: adj. (playing a part; profane under a religious appearance — rendering Hebrew chaneph)
etymology: Greek hupokrites, a stage-player, one who answers from under a mask. The Hebrew chaneph is stronger and darker: soiled with sin, profane, godless under a cover.
biblical_def: Hypocritical in the Old Testament translates a Hebrew word that means profane or polluted — not merely inconsistent but godless beneath a covering. David describes his tormentors: “With hypocritical mockers in feasts, they gnashed upon me with their teeth” (Psa 35:16). Isaiah applies the word to a whole people under judgment: “I will send him against an hypocritical nation, and against the people of my wrath will I give him a charge, to take the spoil, and to take the prey” (Isa 10:6). That is the terrible use. A nation may keep its temple, its sacrifices and its feasts, and be called hypocritical by God because the religion covers a heart at war with Him. The Lord Jesus names the same condition in its most respectable form: “Even so ye also outwardly appear righteous unto men, but within ye are full of hypocrisy and iniquity” (Mat 23:28). And Bildad, for all his hardness toward Job, states the settled truth: “So are the paths of all that forget God; and the hypocrite's hope shall perish” (Job 8:13). The hypocrite is not a man who fails to live up to his profession — that describes every Christian — but a man whose profession is the covering rather than the confession of what he is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hypocritical as counterfeiting a good character; dissembling; insincere; applied to one who assumes an appearance of piety and virtue when he is destitute of them.
webster_full: HYPOCRIT'ICAL, a. Counterfeiting a good character which one has not; dissembling; insincere.
2. Proceeding from hypocrisy, or marking hypocrisy; as, hypocritical professions.
HYP'OCRITE, n. One who feigns to be what he is not; one who has the form of godliness without the power, or who assumes an appearance of piety and virtue when he is destitute of true religion.
HYPOC'RISY, n. Simulation; a feigning to be what one is not; particularly, the assuming of a false appearance of virtue or religion.
scriptures: Psalm 35:16
With hypocritical mockers in feasts, they gnashed upon me with their teeth.
Isaiah 10:6

I will send him against an hypocritical nation, and against the people of my wrath will I give him a charge, to take the spoil, and to take the prey, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets.
Matthew 23:28
Even so ye also outwardly appear righteous unto men, but within ye are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.
Job 8:13
So are the paths of all that forget God; and the hypocrite's hope shall perish:
corruption_summary: The charge of hypocrisy is turned against anyone who holds a standard he has not perfectly kept, so that the word now condemns conviction instead of pretence.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest use of the word today is an accusation aimed at any Christian who names a sin he has himself committed, or who upholds a standard he has failed. That is not what Scripture means. A man who confesses a standard, breaks it, and repents is not a hypocrite; he is a sinner behaving as a believer ought. The hypocrite of Matthew 23 is the man who outwardly appears righteous unto men while inwardly full of iniquity — whose religion is the mask, not the confession. Redefining the word as it is now used has a convenient effect: it silences moral speech altogether, since no one may name a sin he has not perfectly overcome.

The second thing the word exposes is corporate. Isaiah 10:6 calls an entire covenant nation hypocritical, with its worship still running, and sends a pagan empire against it. That judgment falls on a people whose religion had become a covering over injustice, and the prophets are explicit about what was under the covering — the fatherless not judged, the widow's cause not heard, hands full of blood. A church or a nation may keep every ordinance and be under this word. The remedy is never to abandon the forms but to be what the forms declare, and to begin the reckoning at the house of God.
roots_summary: Hebrew chaneph (H2611), profane, polluted, godless — rendered hypocritical in Psalm 35:16 and Isaiah 10:6; Greek hupokrisis (G5272) and hupokrites (G5273), the stage-player.
roots_lines: Hebrew chaneph (H2611) — soiled with sin, profane; Job 8:13, Psalm 35:16, Isaiah 10:6.
Hebrew chanaph (H2610) — to be polluted, defiled; used of a land defiled by bloodshed, Numbers 35:33.
Greek hupokrites (G5273) — an actor under an assumed character; the Lord's word for the scribes and Pharisees.
Greek hupokrisis (G5272) — the playing of the part; Matthew 23:28, Galatians 2:13, 1 Timothy 4:2.
The Hebrew is heavier than the Greek: not merely feigning, but profane beneath the appearance.
usage: “An hypocritical nation” — the temple still running, the heart at war.
“Outwardly appear righteous unto men, but within…” — the mask defined.
“The hypocrite's hope shall perish” — the one hope that has nothing under it.

pos: n. pl. (those who hate; in Romans, haters of God — rendering Greek theostugeis and Hebrew sane)
etymology: From hate, Old English hatian. The Greek compound in Romans 1:30, theostuges, joins theos (God) with a root meaning to abhor — hateful to God, and hating God.
biblical_def: Haters in Scripture is used chiefly in one direction: men hating God. Paul's indictment of the race includes the phrase in its bare form: “Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents” (Rom 1:30). The list is not describing a criminal class but the natural condition of man without God, and haters of God stands in the middle of it as the root from which the rest grow. The Psalmist speaks of the same men and of what they forfeited: “The haters of the LORD should have submitted themselves unto him: but their time should have endured for ever” (Psa 81:15). The Lord Jesus warned that the hatred would be transferred to His people: “If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you” (Joh 15:18). And John draws the line that tests every profession from the other side: “If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?” (1Jn 4:20). Hatred of God is the natural man's posture; hatred of a brother in the church is proof that the natural man is still in possession.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hater as one who hates; one who dislikes with strong aversion; and hatred as great dislike or aversion, particularly that which is settled and rooted.
webster_full: HA'TER, n. One who hates; one who dislikes with strong aversion.

HA'TRED, n. Great dislike or aversion; hate; enmity. Hatred is an aversion to evil, and may spring from utter disapprobation, as the hatred of vice; or it may spring from offenses or injuries done by fellow men.
HATE, v.t. To dislike greatly; to have a great aversion to.
2. In Scripture, to love less; but also, in its proper force, to regard with settled enmity, as the wicked hate God.
scriptures: Romans 1:30
Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents,
Psalm 81:15
The haters of the LORD should have submitted themselves unto him: but their time should have endured for ever.
John 15:18
If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you.
1 John 4:20
If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?
corruption_summary: Enmity against God is denied outright, and men who have never submitted to Him are described as merely uninformed or indifferent.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern account of unbelief is that it is intellectual or circumstantial — a want of evidence, an unhappy experience with religion, an accident of upbringing. Romans 1 says otherwise, and the phrase haters of God is the point at which the account becomes offensive to modern ears. Paul is not describing unusually wicked men; he is describing what the race is by nature, having held the truth in unrighteousness. The doctrine is not cruelty but diagnosis, and it explains what no other account can: why the natural man is not moved to submission by evidence, and why regeneration, not persuasion alone, is required.

John 15:18 keeps the church from misreading its own experience. When the world hates a Christian, the hatred is not first personal; it hated Christ before it hated him. That knowledge protects a believer from two errors — the self-pity that treats opposition as unique injustice, and the anxiety that treats it as proof of some failure of tact. But 1 John 4:20 turns the knife the other way and forbids any comfortable use of the doctrine. A man who claims to love God and hates his brother is called a liar in plain words. The hatred that damns is not confined to the world outside; it can be sitting in a pew.
roots_summary: Greek theostuges (G2319), hater of God — Romans 1:30 only; miseo (G3404), to hate; Hebrew sane (H8130), to hate personally.
roots_lines: Greek theostuges (G2319) — hateful to God, hater of God; Romans 1:30, its only occurrence.
Greek miseo (G3404) — to hate; John 15:18-25, 1 John 4:20, and of the world's settled attitude to Christ.
Hebrew sane (H8130) — to hate personally; Psalm 81:15, Deuteronomy 7:10, Proverbs 8:36.
Psalm 81:15 shows what the hatred cost: the haters of the LORD should have submitted, and their time should have endured for ever.
John 15:25 traces the world's hatred of Christ to prophecy: they hated me without a cause.
usage: “Haters of God” — the root in the middle of Paul's list.
“It hated me before it hated you” — the hatred is not first personal.
“I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar” — the test runs both ways.

pos: n. pl. (empty talk; fruitless discussion — rendering Greek kenophoniai)
etymology: Imitative, from the sound of meaningless speech. The Greek kenophonia is compounded of kenos (empty) and phone (sound) — empty noise.
biblical_def: Babblings is Paul's word for religious talk that carries nothing, and both occurrences are warnings to a young minister. “O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called” (1Ti 6:20). “But shun profane and vain babblings: for they will increase unto more ungodliness” (2Ti 2:16). The Greek word means empty sound, and the two adjectives are exact: the talk is profane because it handles holy things without reverence, and vain because it arrives nowhere. Paul says something about it that is easy to miss — it does not stay level. Vain babbling will increase unto more ungodliness; the appetite for novel talk grows, and the men who feed it move steadily away. He describes the same drift elsewhere: “From which some having swerved have turned aside unto vain jangling” (1Ti 1:6), and orders Titus to “avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain” (Tit 3:9). Against all of it stands the positive command: keep that which is committed to thy trust. A minister is a trustee of a deposit, and his defence against fashionable emptiness is not cleverness but custody.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines babbling as idle talk; senseless prattle; and, in the Scriptures, vain and unprofitable discourse about religion which increases to ungodliness.
webster_full: BAB'BLING, n. Foolish talk; senseless prattle.
BAB'BLE, v.i. To utter words imperfectly or indistinctly; to talk idly or irrationally; to talk much; to prate.
2. To tell secrets; to utter what ought to be kept secret.
VAIN, a. Empty; worthless; having no substance, value or importance.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 6:20
O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:
2 Timothy 2:16
But shun profane and vain babblings: for they will increase unto more ungodliness.
1 Timothy 1:6
From which some having swerved have turned aside unto vain jangling;
Titus 3:9
But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain.
corruption_summary: Endless religious talk is mistaken for theological seriousness, and the deposit a minister was charged to keep is exchanged for the discussion of it.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's two commands to Timothy stand side by side: keep that which is committed to thy trust, and avoid profane and vain babblings. They are one instruction. The trust is a fixed deposit of doctrine handed down, and the babbling is anything that occupies a minister's attention in place of keeping it. The danger is not that the talk is obviously wicked — it is religious, learned, and often stimulating — but that it is empty sound, and that a man can spend a ministry on it and hand nothing on. The test Paul gives is fruit: does it profit, or is it unprofitable and vain?

The warning that it will increase unto more ungodliness deserves particular weight, because it denies that vain talk is harmlessly static. It has a direction. Paul's phrase in the same verse, oppositions of science falsely so called, names the mechanism of his day — a knowledge that presented itself as advanced and set itself against the deposit. Every generation produces its version, and the pattern holds: what begins as an interesting question ends as a departure. Titus 3:9 gives the pastoral rule in one word, avoid; not refute at length, not host indefinitely, but avoid.
roots_summary: Greek kenophonia (G2757), empty sound, vain babbling — 1 Timothy 6:20, 2 Timothy 2:16; mataiologia (G3150), vain jangling; bebelos (G952), profane.
roots_lines: Greek kenophonia (G2757) — empty sounding, fruitless discussion; 1 Timothy 6:20 and 2 Timothy 2:16 only.
Greek mataiologia (G3150) — vain talking, jangling; 1 Timothy 1:6, with mataiologos (G3151) in Titus 1:10.
Greek bebelos (G952) — profane, unhallowed; the adjective in both babbling verses, and of Esau in Hebrews 12:16.
Greek paratheke — the deposit committed to trust; the thing Timothy is to keep against all of it.
2 Timothy 2:16 supplies the reason for shunning rather than debating: such talk increases unto more ungodliness.
usage: “Keep that which is committed to thy trust” — custody, not cleverness.
“They will increase unto more ungodliness” — vain talk has a direction.
“Unprofitable and vain” — the test is fruit.

pos: n. (bitter anger; rage — rendering Hebrew marar, to be bitter)
etymology: Greek chole, bile, through Latin cholera. The older physicians reckoned anger a disorder of the bile, and the English word keeps that image; the Hebrew behind it means simply to be bitter.
biblical_def: Choler is bitter, rising anger, and the Authorized Version uses it twice, both times in Daniel and both times of a king. Of the he goat that ran upon the ram: “And I saw him come close unto the ram, and he was moved with choler against him, and smote the ram, and brake his two horns… and there was none that could deliver the ram out of his hand” (Dan 8:7). And of the king of the south: “the king of the south shall be moved with choler, and shall come forth and fight with him, even with the king of the north: and he shall set forth a great multitude; but the multitude shall be given into his hand” (Dan 11:11). Both passages are prophecy of empires, and in both the anger produces action — and in both the outcome is already appointed. The king moved with choler sets forth a great multitude, and the multitude is given into his hand, that is, into the hand of the other. This is Daniel's constant lesson: the rage of kings is real and is not sovereign. Against it Scripture sets the man who governs himself: “He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city” (Pro 16:32), and James' verdict on every such passion: “the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” (Jas 1:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines choler as the bile; and figuratively, anger, wrath, irritation of the passions, from the ancient notion that anger arises from an excess of bile.
webster_full: CHOL'ER, n. The bile; formerly reckoned one of the four humors of the body.
2. Anger; wrath; irascibility; irritation of the passions.
CHOL'ERIC, a. Abounding with choler; easily irritated; irascible; inclined to anger.
2. Angry; indicating anger; excited by anger; as a choleric speech.
scriptures: Daniel 8:7

And I saw him come close unto the ram, and he was moved with choler against him, and smote the ram, and brake his two horns: and there was no power in the ram to stand before him, but he cast him down to the ground, and stamped upon him: and there was none that could deliver the ram out of his hand.
Daniel 11:11

And the king of the south shall be moved with choler, and shall come forth and fight with him, even with the king of the north: and he shall set forth a great multitude; but the multitude shall be given into his hand.
Proverbs 16:32
He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.
James 1:20
For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.
corruption_summary: Anger is treated as a force that must be discharged rather than ruled, and the rage of the powerful is mistaken for strength.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 16:32 measures greatness in the exact opposite direction from the world's reckoning: the man slow to anger is better than the mighty, and the man who rules his own spirit than the man who takes a city. Daniel supplies the illustration. Kings moved with choler take cities and lose them again, and the whole vision is designed to show a captive people that the Most High ruleth in the kingdom of men. Where rage is admired as force, this proverb sounds like weakness; it is in fact the harder conquest, and the only one that lasts.

The therapeutic account fails at the same point from the other side. Anger is said to be an energy that must be expressed or it will do damage within, so that discharge becomes health and self-government becomes repression. James answers with a flat verdict: the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God. Not sometimes; not unless well directed. The wrath of man produces nothing God is after, and the counsel of Scripture is to be slow to it, to let the sun go down on none of it, and to leave vengeance with the One to whom it belongs. There is a righteous anger — the Lord Himself looked round about on them with anger, being grieved — but it is grieved, and it is at sin, and it does not need to be discharged upon a brother to be satisfied.
roots_summary: Hebrew marar (H4843), to be bitter, enraged — Daniel 8:7 and 11:11; chemah (H2534), heat, fury; charon (H2740), a burning of anger.
roots_lines: Hebrew marar (H4843) — to be bitter; the verb behind moved with choler in Daniel 8:7 and 11:11.
Hebrew chemah (H2534) — heat, hot displeasure, fury; the common Old Testament word for burning anger.
Hebrew charon (H2740) — a burning of anger; used chiefly of the fierce wrath of the LORD.
Greek chole (G5521) — gall, bile; the source of the English word, from the old physiology of the humours.
Daniel shows the rage of kings producing real violence and still serving the appointed end: the multitude is given into his hand.
usage: “Moved with choler” — twice in Daniel, twice of a king, twice under a decree.
“He that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city” — the harder conquest.
“The wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” — a flat verdict.

pos: adj. (severe, harsh, exacting — rendering Greek austeros)
etymology: Greek austeros, harsh or rough to the taste, as unripe fruit; hence severe in manner. The Latin and English keep the sense of sternness without mercy.
biblical_def: Austere occurs twice, in one place, and it is a slander. In the parable of the pounds the servant who hid his lord's money explains himself: “For I feared thee, because thou art an austere man: thou takest up that thou layedst not down, and reapest that thou didst not sow” (Luk 19:21). The lord does not accept the description as true; He takes it as the servant's own testimony and judges him by it: “Out of thine own mouth will I judge thee, thou wicked servant. Thou knewest that I was an austere man, taking up that I laid not down, and reaping that I did not sow” (Luk 19:22), and then the crushing question: “Wherefore then gavest not thou my money into the bank, that at my coming I might have required mine own with usury?” (Luk 19:23). The reasoning is exact. If the servant truly believed his master to be hard, that belief should have produced more diligence, not less. The excuse convicts him because it is not the reason for his idleness but the cover for it. Matthew's parallel parable has the same slander in different words — “I knew thee that thou art an hard man, reaping where thou hast not sown” (Mat 25:24). Wrong thoughts of God are never merely intellectual; they are always used to excuse something.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines austere as severe; harsh; rigid; stern; applied to men and their actions; and, of taste, sour with astringency, as unripe fruit.
webster_full: AUSTE'RE, a. Severe; harsh; rigid; stern; applied to men or their actions.
2. Sour with astringency; harsh to the taste; as austere fruit.
AUSTER'ITY, n. Severity of manners or life; rigor; strictness; harsh discipline.
HARD, a. In a moral sense, oppressive; rigorous; severe; cruel.
scriptures: Luke 19:21
For I feared thee, because thou art an austere man: thou takest up that thou layedst not down, and reapest that thou didst not sow.
Luke 19:22
And he saith unto him, Out of thine own mouth will I judge thee, thou wicked servant. Thou knewest that I was an austere man, taking up that I laid not down, and reaping that I did not sow:
Luke 19:23
Wherefore then gavest not thou my money into the bank, that at my coming I might have required mine own with usury?
Matthew 25:24
Then he which had received the one talent came and said, Lord, I knew thee that thou art an hard man, reaping where thou hast not sown, and gathering where thou hast not strawed:
corruption_summary: God is charged with harshness, and the charge is then used as a reason for doing nothing with what He has given.
corruption_paragraphs: The unprofitable servant is the perfect specimen of a permanent human strategy: form a low opinion of God, then plead that opinion as an excuse. He calls his lord austere, taking up what he laid not down. It is a lie about the master — the man had been given a pound he never earned, by a lord who trusted him with it — and the lie has a purpose, which is to make his idleness look like caution. Every complaint that God's commands are too hard, His standard unreasonable, His providence unfair, should be examined for the same structure. What is the accusation being used to excuse?

The lord's answer is the sharpest thing in the parable and destroys the excuse from inside. If the servant really believed his master hard and exacting, that belief demanded more effort — at the very least, the bank. The excuse fails on its own terms, which shows it was never a belief at all but a cover. And this is the mercy in the passage as well as the severity: no one at that judgment will be condemned for a sincere misunderstanding of God. The servant is judged out of his own mouth, by a standard he himself professed.
roots_summary: Greek austeros (G840), harsh, severe, rough to the taste — Luke 19:21-22 only; skleros (G4642), hard, in the parallel of Matthew 25:24.
roots_lines: Greek austeros (G840) — severe, harsh; Luke 19:21 and 19:22 only, both on the lips of the unprofitable servant.
Greek skleros (G4642) — hard, stiff, harsh; Matthew 25:24 in the parallel parable, and of the hard sayings of Jude 15.
Greek mna (G3414) — the pound entrusted to each servant in Luke 19, a sum the servant had not earned.
The word is originally of taste — unripe fruit, sour and rough — and passes from the palate to the character.
Neither passage endorses the description; both record it as a servant's slander used as an excuse.
usage: “Because thou art an austere man” — a lie told about the master to cover the servant.
“Out of thine own mouth will I judge thee” — the excuse becomes the standard.
“Wherefore then gavest not thou my money into the bank?” — the excuse fails on its own terms.

pos: adj. and adv. (without cause; groundless; undeserved — rendering Hebrew chinnam)
etymology: From cause and the ending -less. The Hebrew chinnam means gratis — without cost, without reason, for nothing; the same word used of what is given freely and of what is done without ground.
biblical_def: Causeless renders a Hebrew word meaning for nothing, and Scripture uses it in two directions. Solomon gives the promise that has quieted many a fearful believer: “As the bird by wandering, as the swallow by flying, so the curse causeless shall not come” (Pro 26:2). A curse without ground has no power to land; it flits past like a bird that will not settle, because it is not God who sent it and He alone gives words their effect. Abigail uses the word of bloodshed, restraining David from a slaughter he would have regretted all his life: “That this shall be no grief unto thee, nor offence of heart unto my lord, either that thou hast shed blood causeless, or that my lord hath avenged himself” (1Sa 25:31). The same Hebrew word describes the hatred borne against the righteous: “neither let them wink with the eye that hate me without a cause” (Psa 35:19), which the Lord Jesus applied to Himself: “this cometh to pass, that the word might be fulfilled that is written in their law, They hated me without a cause” (Joh 15:25). So the word covers a curse that cannot land, blood that must not be shed, and a hatred that had no ground at all — the hatred that crucified the Lord of glory.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines causeless as having no cause or occasion; without just ground, reason or motive; as causeless hatred, or a causeless curse.
webster_full: CAUSELESS, a. Having no cause or producing agent.
2. Without just ground, reason or motive; as causeless hatred; causeless fear.
CAUSELESSLY, adv. Without cause or reason.
CURSE, n. Malediction; the expression of a wish of evil to another.
scriptures: Proverbs 26:2
As the bird by wandering, as the swallow by flying, so the curse causeless shall not come.
1 Samuel 25:31
That this shall be no grief unto thee, nor offence of heart unto my lord, either that thou hast shed blood causeless, or that my lord hath avenged himself:
Psalm 35:19
Let not them that are mine enemies wrongfully rejoice over me: neither let them wink with the eye that hate me without a cause.
John 15:25
But this cometh to pass, that the word might be fulfilled that is written in their law, They hated me without a cause.
corruption_summary: Fear of words and curses is nursed where Scripture dismisses them, while genuine hatred against the righteous is explained away as something they must have provoked.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 26:2 is a standing rebuke to superstition, including the superstition that circulates in Christian dress. Where believers are taught to fear generational curses, spoken words, hexes, or the malice of enemies as forces with power of their own, Solomon answers that a curse without ground does not land; it wanders like a bird that finds no perch. God governs what befalls His people, and no word spoken against them has any force He does not give it. The proper fear of the Christian is toward God alone, and the counterfeit fear that scans the past for curses to break is not faith but paganism with a vocabulary.

The second and opposite error is to assume that hostility against the righteous must always have been earned. Sometimes it has — Peter warns believers not to suffer as busybodies or evildoers and then claim the blessing of persecution. But John 15:25 records a hatred with no ground whatever, aimed at the only man who never gave one. Where the church assumes that all opposition is deserved, it will counsel its own into endless self-suspicion; where it assumes none is, it will never repent of the offences it actually gives. Abigail's words to David show the discernment required: she stopped a righteous man from shedding blood causeless, and she did it while granting the wrong he had suffered was real.
roots_summary: Hebrew chinnam (H2600), gratis, for nothing, without cause — Proverbs 26:2, 1 Samuel 25:31, Psalm 35:19; from chen (H2580), favour, grace.
roots_lines: Hebrew chinnam (H2600) — without cost or cause; Proverbs 26:2, Psalm 35:19, Psalm 69:4, Job 2:3.
Hebrew chen (H2580) — grace, favour; the root, so the same word can mean freely given and groundlessly done.
Greek dorean (G1432) — freely, without a cause; the Septuagint word behind John 15:25, and rendered freely in Romans 3:24.
John 15:25 quotes Psalm 35:19 and Psalm 69:4 of the hatred borne by Christ.
The same root that says men hated Him without a cause says sinners are justified freely by His grace.
usage: “The curse causeless shall not come” — it wanders like a bird and finds no perch.
“That thou hast shed blood causeless” — Abigail stops a righteous man in time.
“They hated me without a cause” — the one hatred that was wholly groundless.

pos: n. pl. (those who corrupt others; agents of decay — rendering Hebrew shachath)
etymology: Latin corrumpere, to break utterly, to spoil. The Hebrew shachath means to decay and, causatively, to ruin — the corrupter is not merely corrupt but ruins what he touches.
biblical_def: Corrupters names men who do not merely rot but spread the rot. Isaiah opens his prophecy with it: “Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, a seed of evildoers, children that are corrupters: they have forsaken the LORD, they have provoked the Holy One of Israel unto anger, they are gone away backward” (Isa 1:4). Jeremiah says the same of his generation: “They are all grievous revolters, walking with slanders: they are brass and iron; they are all corrupters” (Jer 6:28). In both places the charge is laid against the covenant people, not against the heathen, and in both the corruption is active — these are children who make others what they are. Paul brings the word into the ministry, where its damage is greatest: “For we are not as many, which corrupt the word of God: but as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God speak we in Christ” (2Co 2:17). The Greek there is a merchant's word, of a trader who waters the wine before selling it — the word of God adulterated for gain. And the final judgment falls on the great corrupter of nations: God “hath judged the great whore, which did corrupt the earth with her fornication, and hath avenged the blood of his servants at her hand” (Rev 19:2). Corruption in Scripture always spreads, and God always finally arrests it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a corrupter as one who corrupts; one who vitiates or taints; one who bribes, or destroys purity of principles and morals in others.
webster_full: CORRUPT'ER, n. One who corrupts; one who vitiates or taints; one who bribes; that which depraves or destroys integrity.
CORRUPT', v.t. To change from a sound to a putrid state; to vitiate or deprave; to destroy purity of principles.
2. To infect with errors or the vices of others.
CORRUP'TION, n. The act of corrupting, or state of being corrupt; putrescence; depravity; perversion of principles.
scriptures: Isaiah 1:4

Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, a seed of evildoers, children that are corrupters: they have forsaken the LORD, they have provoked the Holy One of Israel unto anger, they are gone away backward.
Jeremiah 6:28
They are all grievous revolters, walking with slanders: they are brass and iron; they are all corrupters.
2 Corinthians 2:17
For we are not as many, which corrupt the word of God: but as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God speak we in Christ.
Revelation 19:2
For true and righteous are his judgments: for he hath judged the great whore, which did corrupt the earth with her fornication, and hath avenged the blood of his servants at her hand.
corruption_summary: Corruption is treated as a private failing that harms no one else, when Scripture consistently describes it as contagious and names its agents.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah does not say the nation was corrupt; he says its children were corrupters, and the difference is the whole point. Sin propagates. A man's private compromise becomes his household's norm, his church's tolerance, and his nation's law, and Scripture treats him accordingly. The modern maxim that private conduct concerns no one else is refuted by the plain sociology of the prophets, who indict a whole people for what began in individual households. Where a church cannot say who is corrupting whom, it has already lost the ability to discipline anything.

Second Corinthians 2:17 names the corrupter the church most needs to fear — the man who adulterates the word of God. Paul's word is drawn from the wine trade, where a merchant thins his stock and sells it at full strength's price. The trade continues. A doctrine softened to keep hearers, a text handled to avoid offence, a promise detached from the command that governs it: each is watered wine, and the buyers cannot tell until they need the strength that is not there. Paul's alternative is set out in three phrases — of sincerity, of God, in the sight of God — which together describe a man who preaches as though the Owner of the deposit were standing beside him, because He is.
roots_summary: Hebrew shachath (H7843), to decay, ruin, corrupt — Isaiah 1:4, Jeremiah 6:28; Greek kapeleuo (G2585), to peddle adulterated goods, in 2 Corinthians 2:17; phtheiro (G5351), to spoil.
roots_lines: Hebrew shachath (H7843) — to decay, and causatively to ruin; Isaiah 1:4, Genesis 6:12 of all flesh corrupting its way.
Greek kapeleuo (G2585) — to hawk, to trade in adulterated goods; 2 Corinthians 2:17, its only occurrence.
Greek phtheiro (G5351) — to spoil, corrupt, destroy; 1 Corinthians 15:33, 2 Corinthians 11:3, Revelation 19:2.
The Hebrew is active: a corrupter does not merely rot, he ruins what he handles.
Isaiah 1:4 and Jeremiah 6:28 both lay the charge against the covenant people, not against the nations.
usage: “Children that are corrupters” — not merely corrupt, but spreading it.
“Many, which corrupt the word of God” — the merchant's watered wine.
“In the sight of God speak we in Christ” — the preacher's only safe posture.

pos: adv. and adj. (out of rank; irregularly; idly — rendering Greek ataktos)
etymology: From dis- and order. The Greek ataktos is a military word: a soldier out of rank, one who will not keep his place in the line.
biblical_def: Disorderly in the New Testament is a soldier's word applied to a church. Paul commands: “Now we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us” (2Th 3:6). He then names the specific disorder: “we hear that there are some which walk among you disorderly, working not at all, but are busybodies” (2Th 3:11). The two go together with grim consistency — the man who has left his own work invariably takes up other men's. Paul appeals to his own example: “yourselves know how ye ought to follow us: for we behaved not ourselves disorderly among you” (2Th 3:7), and he had laboured night and day rather than be chargeable to any. He then gives a rule the church has never been able to soften: “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10). Note the exactness of the wording: not could not work, but would not. The passage assumes a church that provides for widows, the sick, and the genuinely destitute; it addresses the man who is able and unwilling. And the discipline prescribed is neither expulsion nor indulgence but withdrawal — a measured distance intended to shame him, while still counting him a brother.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines disorderly as being without proper order; irregular; unruly; contrary to rule or law; and, in the Scriptures, walking out of the appointed order of the church.
webster_full: DISOR'DERLY, a. Being without proper order; irregular; immethodical; confused.
2. Unruly; contrary to law; violating rule or law; as disorderly persons.
DISOR'DERLY, adv. Without order or rule; irregularly; confusedly.
BUS'YBODY, n. One who officiously concerns himself with the affairs of others; a meddling person.
scriptures: 2 Thessalonians 3:6
Now we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us.
2 Thessalonians 3:11
For we hear that there are some which walk among you disorderly, working not at all, but are busybodies.
2 Thessalonians 3:7
For yourselves know how ye ought to follow us: for we behaved not ourselves disorderly among you;
2 Thessalonians 3:10
For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.
corruption_summary: Church discipline is abandoned as unloving, and the plain apostolic distinction between the man who cannot work and the man who will not is erased in both directions.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul commands withdrawal from a disorderly brother in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ — the weightiest formula he uses — and modern congregations quietly decline. The reasons given are that discipline is judgmental, that the offence is minor, or that the man will simply go elsewhere. All three are answered by the text: the apostle calls this a command, applies it to idleness rather than scandal, and prescribes a remedy short of excommunication. Withdrawal is a graded measure. It is designed to be felt, and its aim is stated plainly — that he may be ashamed, and that he be counted not as an enemy but admonished as a brother.

The rule if any would not work, neither should he eat is abused from both sides. Some quote it against the poor generally, ignoring that Scripture commands the gleaning corner, the third-year tithe, the care of widows indeed, and the relief of the brethren in famine. Others treat any application of it as cruelty, which leaves a congregation unable to distinguish the disabled from the idle and finally exhausts its ability to help either. Paul's wording is careful and the church should be equally careful: the man in view is able and unwilling, and the same apostle who wrote this verse organized a collection for the poor saints at Jerusalem.

The connection Paul draws between idleness and busybodying deserves its own note. Working not at all, but are busybodies — the energy does not disappear when a man abandons his own labour; it is redirected into the affairs of others. Much of what troubles congregations under the name of concern is simply this: unemployed strength looking for an object. The apostolic remedy is not a rebuke about meddling but a return to honest work, that with quietness they work, and eat their own bread.
roots_summary: Greek ataktos (G814), disorderly, out of rank — 2 Thessalonians 3:6, 3:11; atakteo (G812), to behave disorderly — 2 Thessalonians 3:7; periergazomai (G4020), to be a busybody.
roots_lines: Greek ataktos (G814) — disorderly, out of rank; 2 Thessalonians 3:6 and 3:11, a military figure applied to church members.
Greek atakteo (G812) — to act irregularly; 2 Thessalonians 3:7, its only occurrence.
Greek periergazomai (G4020) — to bustle about other people's business; 2 Thessalonians 3:11, a play on the word for working.
Greek stello (G4724) — to withdraw, keep away from; the discipline commanded in 2 Thessalonians 3:6.
The soldier out of rank endangers the line, not only himself — which is why the church, not merely the man, is addressed.
usage: “Withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly” — a command, not a suggestion.
“Working not at all, but are busybodies” — idle strength finds an object.
“If any would not work, neither should he eat” — would not, and the word is deliberate.

pos: n. (speaking against; gainsaying; dispute — rendering Greek antilogia)
etymology: Latin contradictio, a speaking against, from contra and dicere. The Greek antilogia is the same compound in Greek — a word set against a word.
biblical_def: Contradiction in the Authorized Version is not logical inconsistency but speaking against — hostile gainsaying. Hebrews uses it of what Christ endured: “For consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, lest ye be wearied and faint in your minds” (Heb 12:3). The verse is a remedy for exhaustion. Believers under pressure are told to reckon up what He bore, and to measure their own opposition against it. The context supplies the pattern: He “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God” (Heb 12:2) — endurance sustained by a joy ahead and vindicated by a throne. The same epistle uses the word in an entirely different key: “And without all contradiction the less is blessed of the better” (Heb 7:7), meaning without any possible dispute, in the argument for the superiority of Melchisedec's priesthood to Levi's. And in a third place the writer notes that an oath ends strife: “an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife” (Heb 6:16). So the word covers what men say against Christ, what no man can say against a plain truth, and the settling of disputes by an oath from the mouth of God Himself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines contradiction as an assertion of the contrary to what has been said or affirmed; denial; opposition; and also, inconsistency between two propositions.
webster_full: CONTRADIC'TION, n. An assertion of the contrary to what has been said or affirmed; denial; contrary declaration.
2. Opposition, whether by words or actions.
3. Inconsistency; incongruity; that which implies opposition; as, a contradiction in terms.
GAINSAY', v.t. To contradict; to oppose in words; to deny or declare not to be true.
scriptures: Hebrews 12:3
For consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, lest ye be wearied and faint in your minds.
Hebrews 12:2
Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.
Hebrews 7:7
And without all contradiction the less is blessed of the better.
Hebrews 6:16
For men verily swear by the greater: and an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife.
corruption_summary: Opposition to Christ is reinterpreted as honest inquiry, and the weariness of believers under sustained contradiction is treated as a failure of nerve rather than a burden Christ Himself carried.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 12:3 assumes that faithful men grow weary and faint in their minds under sustained gainsaying, and it does not scold them for it. That is worth noticing in a church culture where discouragement is often treated as spiritual failure. The remedy given is not to try harder or to feel differently but to consider him — to reckon up deliberately the contradiction Christ endured, which was greater in kind and in degree, from those He came to save, and endured to the end. Endurance in Scripture is fed by contemplation of Christ, not by exhortation to endure.

The word also exposes a habit of speech that flatters opposition. Sustained public argument against Christ and His word is frequently presented as inquiry, and the church is urged to receive it as such. Some of it is; honest questions deserve honest answers and Scripture never fears them. But Hebrews names a category of speaking-against that is not inquiry at all, and it was aimed at the Lord by men who had seen His works. To call every contradiction a question is to lose the ability to recognize opposition when it comes, and to leave believers puzzled at their own weariness.
roots_summary: Greek antilogia (G485), a speaking against, gainsaying, dispute — Hebrews 6:16, 7:7, 12:3, Jude 11; from anti (against) and logos (word).
roots_lines: Greek antilogia (G485) — contradiction, gainsaying, strife; Hebrews 6:16, 7:7, 12:3, and Jude 11 of the gainsaying of Core.
Greek antilego (G483) — to speak against; Luke 2:34 of the Child set for a sign spoken against, Acts 28:22, Titus 1:9.
Greek hupomeno (G5278) — to endure, remain under; Hebrews 12:2-3, the verb of both the cross and the contradiction.
Latin contradictio and Greek antilogia are the same compound: a word set against a word.
