Hebrews 7:7 uses the phrase without all contradiction to mean beyond any possible dispute.
usage: “Consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners” — the cure for a fainting mind.
“Without all contradiction the less is blessed of the better” — beyond dispute.
“For the joy that was set before him” — what sustained the enduring.

pos: n. (strife between brethren; contention deliberately sown — rendering Hebrew madon)
etymology: Latin discordia, from dis- (apart) and cor (heart) — hearts pulled apart. The Hebrew madon means contention or quarrel.
biblical_def: Discord is contention between brethren, and Scripture is severe about it because of what it costs and who does it. Solomon describes the worthless man: “Frowardness is in his heart, he deviseth mischief continually; he soweth discord” (Pro 6:14). Then, in the catalogue of what God hates, discord occupies the final and climactic place: “These six things doth the LORD hate: yea, seven are an abomination unto him” (Pro 6:16), and the seventh is “A false witness that speaketh lies, and he that soweth discord among brethren” (Pro 6:19). It is worth weighing that placement. Among proud looks, lying tongues, hands that shed innocent blood and feet swift to mischief, the list ends with the man who sets brothers against each other — and the verb is agricultural. He sows. He does not merely quarrel; he plants, and waits, and lets the crop come up in other men's fields. Paul gives the church its standing order concerning such men: “mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them” (Rom 16:17) — identify them, and keep away. That is not harshness. It is the only protection a congregation has against a sin that operates by concealment.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines discord as disagreement among persons or things; variance; opposition; contention; strife; and, in the Scriptures, the setting at variance of brethren.
webster_full: DIS'CORD, n. Disagreement among persons or things. Between persons, difference of opinions; variance; opposition; contention; strife; any disagreement which produces angry passions.
2. In music, disagreement of sounds; dissonance.
DISCORD'ANT, a. Disagreeing; incongruous; contradictory; being at variance.
SOW, v.t. To scatter seed for growth; hence, to spread; to propagate; as, to sow discord.
scriptures: Proverbs 6:19
A false witness that speaketh lies, and he that soweth discord among brethren.
Proverbs 6:14
Frowardness is in his heart, he deviseth mischief continually; he soweth discord.
Proverbs 6:16
These six things doth the LORD hate: yea, seven are an abomination unto him:
Romans 16:17
Now I beseech you, brethren, mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them.
corruption_summary: Sowing discord is renamed as courage or transparency, so that the man dividing a congregation presents himself as the one telling the truth about it.
corruption_paragraphs: The sower of discord never announces himself. He works by degrees — a concern shared in confidence, a question raised about a motive, a report passed on with regret — and by the time the crop is up, no one can say who planted it. This is exactly why Solomon uses the verb sow and why God places the sin at the head of the list of what He hates. It is also why Romans 16:17 commands the church to mark such men. Marking is identification, and identification is the one thing the sin cannot survive; a discord-sower exposed in the open has lost his method.

Scripture is equally clear that not every division is this sin, and the qualification in Romans 16:17 must not be dropped: the men to be marked cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned. The Reformation divided Christendom, and rightly, because the doctrine was at stake. A man who refuses error and thereby divides is not sowing discord; the discord was sown by whoever brought the error in. The test is never whether unity was disturbed but what the disturbance was about — and a man who divides over the truth will be able to name the doctrine, while the sower of discord deals in impressions, motives, and personalities.
roots_summary: Hebrew madon (H4066) and medan (H4090), contention, strife, discord — Proverbs 6:14, 6:19; Greek dichostasia (G1370), division, in Romans 16:17.
roots_lines: Hebrew madon (H4066) — contention, strife; Proverbs 6:14 and 6:19, and often of the brawling woman in Proverbs.
Hebrew medan (H4090) — discord, strife; the parallel form in Proverbs 6:19.
Greek dichostasia (G1370) — division, dissension; Romans 16:17, Galatians 5:20 among the works of the flesh.
Greek skandalon (G4625) — an offence, a trap-stick; the companion word in Romans 16:17.
The verb is agricultural: the sower plants and waits, and the harvest comes up in another man's field.
usage: “He that soweth discord among brethren” — last and climactic in the list of what God hates.
“He deviseth mischief continually” — it is a settled labour, not an outburst.
“Mark them… and avoid them” — identification destroys the method.

pos: n. (deceit for gain; wages kept back wrongfully — rendering Greek apostereo and Hebrew mirmah)
etymology: Latin fraus, deceit, injury. The Hebrew mirmah means treachery or guile; the Greek apostereo means to defraud, to keep back what is another's.
biblical_def: Fraud in Scripture is not a technicality of commerce but a cry that reaches God. James writes: “Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth” (Jas 5:4). Two things are said. The withheld wage itself cries — the injustice has a voice apart from the man who suffered it — and the cries have entered into the ears of the Lord of hosts, the title of God as commander of armies. The Psalmist marks fraud as a settled character: “His mouth is full of cursing and deceit and fraud: under his tongue is mischief and vanity” (Psa 10:7). The law had legislated against exactly this: “Thou shalt not defraud thy neighbour, neither rob him: the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning” (Lev 19:13), and Moses gives the reason with unusual tenderness: “At his day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it; for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it: lest he cry against thee unto the LORD, and it be sin unto thee” (Deu 24:15). The delay is forbidden because the labourer is poor and has set his heart on the money; God legislates with the workman's evening in view.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fraud as deceit; deception; trick; artifice by which the right or interest of another is injured; a stratagem intended to obtain some undue advantage.
webster_full: FRAUD, n. Deceit; deception; trick; artifice by which the right or interest of another is injured.
2. A stratagem intended to obtain some undue advantage; an attempt to gain, or the obtaining of an advantage over another by imposition or immoral means.
DEFRAUD', v.t. To deprive of right, either by obtaining something by deception or artifice, or by taking something wrongfully without the knowledge or consent of the owner.
HIRE, n. Wages; the price or compensation paid for labor or service.
scriptures: James 5:4

Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.
Psalm 10:7
His mouth is full of cursing and deceit and fraud: under his tongue is mischief and vanity.
Leviticus 19:13
Thou shalt not defraud thy neighbour, neither rob him: the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning.
Deuteronomy 24:15
At his day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it; for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it: lest he cry against thee unto the LORD, and it be sin unto thee.
corruption_summary: Fraud is redefined as whatever the law fails to prohibit, so that a wage lawfully withheld is assumed to be lawfully kept.
corruption_paragraphs: James 5:4 addresses employers who had done nothing illegal by the standards of their day — the wages were withheld, not stolen — and calls it fraud. Scripture's standard for commerce is not the statute book but the labourer's condition, and Deuteronomy states it: he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it. The modern arrangement that pays late, structures a man as a contractor to avoid an obligation, or prices a debt so that it can never be discharged, will generally survive legal scrutiny and will not survive this text. The Lord of sabaoth hears the wage itself, and the arrangement that silenced the man does not silence his hire.

There is a second, quieter corruption in the church, which is the assumption that these are civic matters rather than spiritual ones. James is writing to a congregation, and he addresses the rich among them with the same directness Amos used. Where a church regards a member's business dealings as outside its concern while examining his doctrine minutely, it has divided what the Scriptures join. Psalm 10:7 puts fraud with cursing and deceit as the furniture of a wicked mouth; Leviticus puts it beside robbery in one sentence. What a man does with another man's wages is a matter of the first table as well as the second, because the defrauded man cries to God, and God answers.
roots_summary: Greek apostereo (G650), to defraud, keep back — James 5:4, 1 Corinthians 6:7-8, Mark 10:19; Hebrew mirmah (H4820), deceit, guile; ashaq (H6231), to oppress or defraud.
roots_lines: Greek apostereo (G650) — to defraud, deprive; James 5:4, Mark 10:19, 1 Corinthians 6:8 of brethren defrauding brethren.
Hebrew mirmah (H4820) — deceit, treachery, guile; Psalm 10:7, Proverbs 11:1 of the false balance.
Hebrew ashaq (H6231) — to press upon, oppress, defraud; Leviticus 19:13, Malachi 3:5 of those that oppress the hireling in his wages.
Hebrew sabaoth — hosts, armies; James invokes God under His military title precisely here.
The law fixes the deadline at sunset, because the poor man has set his heart on that day's wage.
usage: “Kept back by fraud, crieth” — the wage itself has a voice.
“The wages… shall not abide with thee all night” — the deadline is sunset.
“He is poor, and setteth his heart upon it” — God legislates with the workman's evening in view.

pos: n. (evil report; public disgrace — rendering Hebrew dibbah)
etymology: Latin infamia, from in- (not) and fama (report, fame) — the loss of good report. The Hebrew dibbah means slander or evil report, whether deserved or not.
biblical_def: Infamy is the loss of a good name, and Scripture treats it as a real and heavy loss. Solomon warns the man who spreads another's secret: “Lest he that heareth it put thee to shame, and thine infamy turn not away” (Pro 25:10) — a disgrace that will not leave once it settles. Ezekiel uses the word of a nation stripped and mocked: the mountains of Israel are “taken up in the lips of talkers, and are an infamy of the people” (Eze 36:3). The Hebrew behind it means evil report, and it is the same word used of the slanderous report the ten spies brought back of the land. So infamy can be the just consequence of sin, as in Proverbs, or the unjust portion of God's people in the mouths of their enemies, as in Ezekiel — where the chapter goes on to promise that God will vindicate His own name and cleanse them. Against the whole subject Scripture sets a plain valuation: “A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour rather than silver and gold” (Pro 22:1), and “A good name is better than precious ointment; and the day of death than the day of one's birth” (Ecc 7:1). A reputation is worth guarding, and worth more than money — but not more than obedience, since Christ Himself made Himself of no reputation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines infamy as total loss of reputation; public disgrace; and also the loss of character incident to a conviction of an infamous crime.
webster_full: IN'FAMY, n. Total loss of reputation; public disgrace.
2. Qualities which are detested and despised; qualities notoriously bad and scandalous.
3. In law, that loss of character or public disgrace which a convict incurs, and by which he is rendered incapable of being a witness.
IN'FAMOUS, a. Of ill report; having a reputation of the worst kind; branded with infamy.
scriptures: Proverbs 25:10
Lest he that heareth it put thee to shame, and thine infamy turn not away.
Ezekiel 36:3

Therefore prophesy and say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Because they have made you desolate, and swallowed you up on every side, that ye might be a possession unto the residue of the heathen, and ye are taken up in the lips of talkers, and are an infamy of the people:
Proverbs 22:1
A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour rather than silver and gold.
Ecclesiastes 7:1
A good name is better than precious ointment; and the day of death than the day of one's birth.
corruption_summary: Public disgrace is inflicted as entertainment and preserved indefinitely, while the reputation Scripture calls better than riches is treated as a thing anyone may destroy at will.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 25:10 warns that an infamy, once fastened, may not turn away, and it says so as a caution to the man doing the fastening. Scripture regards the destruction of another's good name as a serious injury, which is why the ninth commandment exists and why the law required two witnesses before a matter was established. The present machinery for spreading an evil report is faster and more permanent than anything Solomon imagined, and it is used casually, for amusement, and without the possibility of correction. A Christian who repeats a report he has not verified has done a thing Scripture treats as a form of theft.

The other side of the word is comfort. Ezekiel 36 finds God's own people an infamy in the lips of talkers — deserved, since their sin had brought them there — and the chapter answers not with a defence of their conduct but with the promise that God will sanctify His great name and cleanse them from all their filthiness. Vindication belongs to God and He undertakes it. This is why a believer may be commanded to entrust his reputation to God rather than to fight for it: our Lord made Himself of no reputation, was numbered with the transgressors, and is now given a name above every name.

roots_lines: Hebrew dibbah (H1681) — defaming, evil report, slander; Proverbs 25:10, Ezekiel 36:3, and Numbers 13:32 of the spies' evil report.
Hebrew shem (H8034) — name, reputation; Proverbs 22:1 and Ecclesiastes 7:1, where a good name outweighs riches and ointment.
Latin infamia — the undoing of fama, report; the word names a loss, not a quality.
Ezekiel 36 answers infamy with God vindicating His own great name, and cleansing His people.
Philippians 2:7 sets the limit on defending one's name: Christ made Himself of no reputation.
usage: “Thine infamy turn not away” — some disgraces do not lift.
“Taken up in the lips of talkers” — a nation made a byword.
“A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches” — and yet not above obedience.

pos: adj. (without hope; past remedy — rendering Hebrew yaash and anash)
etymology: Latin desperatus, from de- and sperare, to hope — the state of one from whom hope has been taken. The Hebrew anash means incurable; it is the word used of the heart in Jeremiah 17:9.
biblical_def: Desperate in the Authorized Version describes a condition past remedy. Job, answering friends who weighed his words as though he were arguing calmly, protests: “Do ye imagine to reprove words, and the speeches of one that is desperate, which are as wind?” (Job 6:26). He asks them to reckon with the state of the man speaking before they parse his sentences — a rebuke every comforter needs. Isaiah uses the word of a harvest that fails: “In the day shalt thou make thy plant to grow, and in the morning shalt thou make thy seed to flourish: but the harvest shall be a heap in the day of grief and of desperate sorrow” (Isa 17:11). The related Hebrew root gives Jeremiah his verdict on the human heart — deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked — where the word means incurable. That is the exact point at which the gospel begins. Scripture does not call the sinner improvable; it calls him incurable, and then supplies not a cure but a new heart. Against desperation the Psalmist speaks to his own soul: “Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God” (Psa 42:5), and Paul draws the line that a believer is never past: “we are perplexed, but not in despair” (2Co 4:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines desperate as without hope; despairing; hopeless; beyond the reach of hope or cure; and, of persons, rash and regardless of danger from despair of safety.
webster_full: DES'PERATE, a. Without hope; despairing.
2. Without care of safety; rash; fearless of danger; as a desperate man.
3. Irretrievable; irrecoverable; beyond the reach of hope; as a desperate case or disease.
DESPERA'TION, n. A despairing; a giving up of hope; hopelessness; despair.
scriptures: Job 6:26
Do ye imagine to reprove words, and the speeches of one that is desperate, which are as wind?
Isaiah 17:11
In the day shalt thou make thy plant to grow, and in the morning shalt thou make thy seed to flourish: but the harvest shall be a heap in the day of grief and of desperate sorrow.
Psalm 42:5
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance.
2 Corinthians 4:8
We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair;
corruption_summary: The heart's condition is called treatable when Scripture calls it incurable, and the sorrow of the afflicted is answered with argument rather than with God.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah's word for the heart is the root of this one: incurable. Every scheme of self-improvement, moral education, or environmental adjustment assumes the opposite — that the material is workable and needs better handling. Scripture's diagnosis is more severe and its remedy correspondingly greater: not therapy but a new heart, not reformation but resurrection. This is why the gospel offends. A man will accept help; he will not easily accept that his case is desperate and that nothing short of God making him new will answer.

Job 6:26 turns the word on the comforters, and the church should feel the edge of it. Job's friends reproved his words while ignoring the man — parsing the speeches of one that is desperate, which are as wind. Words spoken out of anguish are not the same as considered doctrine, and to answer them with argument is to mistake the wound for the argument. Psalm 42 shows the right handling: the Psalmist does not deny that he is cast down; he addresses his own soul, questions his disquiet, and commands it to hope in God. That is not the suppression of grief but its direction, and Paul's perplexed, but not in despair marks the line a believer may reach and not cross.
roots_summary: Hebrew yaash (H2976), to despond, despair — Job 6:26; anash (H605), to be frail, sick, incurable — Isaiah 17:11, Jeremiah 17:9; Greek exaporeomai (G1820), to be utterly without resource.
roots_lines: Hebrew yaash (H2976) — to despond, to be desperate; Job 6:26, 1 Samuel 27:1, Isaiah 57:10.
Hebrew anash (H605) — frail, woeful, incurable; Isaiah 17:11, and Jeremiah 17:9 of the heart desperately wicked.
Greek exaporeomai (G1820) — to be utterly at a loss, in despair; 2 Corinthians 1:8 and 4:8.
Greek aporeo (G639) — to be perplexed; the word Paul sets against despair in 2 Corinthians 4:8.
Latin desperatus — hope taken away; the exact state from which Psalm 42 recalls the soul to God.
usage: “The speeches of one that is desperate, which are as wind” — reckon with the man before the words.
“Desperately wicked” — incurable, and therefore in need of a new heart.
“Perplexed, but not in despair” — the line a believer reaches and does not cross.
